# Simple Classification of Substances

## Core ideas and reasoning

An element contains atoms of one proton number; a compound contains elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. A mixture contains substances physically combined in variable proportions and can often be separated using physical properties. Homogeneous mixtures are uniform on the scale considered; heterogeneous mixtures have distinct phases. Pure substances have characteristic melting and boiling temperatures at a stated pressure, while mixtures commonly show ranges. Impurities often lower and broaden the melting range of a crystalline solid. During melting, energy changes particle arrangement rather than raising the temperature of a pure substance at constant pressure. Use several measurements to support a purity conclusion rather than relying on colour alone. In chromatography a sample separates because its components have differing affinities for the mobile and stationary phases. A single spot under one set of conditions is evidence consistent with purity, not absolute proof. Keep the solvent below the baseline and mark with pencil so the baseline does not dissolve.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Distinguish an element, a compound and a mixture.

An element has one proton-number type, such as copper. A compound has elements chemically combined in fixed proportions, such as water. A mixture has variable proportions, such as salt water.

### Example 2

What generally happens to the melting behaviour of a pure crystalline solid when an impurity is added?

Its melting temperature is usually lowered and the sharp melting point becomes a broader melting range.

### Example 3

Explain why pencil is used for the baseline in paper chromatography.

Graphite does not normally dissolve and travel with the solvent, whereas ink can separate into its own spots and interfere with results.

### Example 4

How would dilute acid distinguish copper(II) oxide from charcoal, both black solids?

Copper(II) oxide dissolves in suitable dilute mineral acid to give a blue copper(II) solution. Charcoal does not dissolve under those conditions.

### Example 5

Classify neutralisation, sublimation, fractional distillation and displacement as chemical or physical changes.

Neutralisation: chemical. Sublimation: physical. Fractional distillation: physical. Displacement reaction: chemical. Chemical changes form new substances; the physical changes separate or change states.

### Example 6

State two physical properties used to assess a substance’s purity.

Melting point and boiling point, measured at stated pressure and compared with characteristic values. Other useful properties include density and refractive index.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
